key_terms.meaning: The set of design work products — data, architecture, interfaces, components, deployment — built from the requirements model and used as the blueprint for code.
A measurable property a design must have, such as maintainability, performance, security, usability or reliability; designs are judged against these, not against looks.
The early design step that fixes the system's major parts, their responsibilities and how they communicate.
Design of each software unit in detail: its operations, internal logic and data structures.
Design of data structures and database schemas that the software will store, read and update.
Each module keeps its internal decisions private and exposes only a small, stable interface.
How strongly the work inside one module belongs together; high cohesion means one module, one job.
How much one module depends on another; low coupling means a change in one module rarely forces a change in another.
Breaking the whole problem into smaller functions, and each function into sub-functions, until each piece is simple enough to design and test.
An architecture that stacks layers, each offering services to the layer above and using only the layer below; a request travels down and a result travels up.
A server holds shared data or services; many clients request them over a network; the protocol between them is the contract.
Filters transform data and pipes pass the stream from one filter to the next; filters do not know who produced or consumes the data.
A named, reusable solution to a recurring design problem, described by its intent, structure and consequences.
A subject keeps a list of observers and notifies all of them when its state changes, so the subject does not need to know who is watching.
One simple front object that offers a small set of operations to a complicated subsystem hiding behind it.
A pattern that splits an application into model (data and rules), view (display) and controller (input handling), so the display can change without touching the logic.

key_terms.term: Rule 1 — place the user in control
key_terms.meaning: The interface lets the user decide what happens next: cancel, undo, choose modes, and it never traps the user in one path.
The static UML view: classes with attributes and operations, joined by associations, generalisations and dependencies with multiplicities.
A UML interaction diagram with objects across the top and time running downwards, showing messages in order.
A column or row in an activity diagram that assigns each action to one responsible actor or department.

takeaways: Design is the translation step: the requirements model says what is needed, the design model says how the software will be built, in five sub-models — data, architecture, interface, component and deployment.
A design choice is never good in the abstract; it is good only when it satisfies the quality attributes that matter for that product.
Abstraction and functional decomposition let you think about a large system at one level at a time, which is the only way a human can hold it in mind.
High cohesion with low coupling is the one-line summary of a maintainable module structure.
Architecture is the set of decisions that are expensive to change later, so it deserves the earliest and most careful thought.
An architectural style is a named template — layered, client-server, pipe-filter — that brings known trade-offs you can argue about before you code.
A pattern is worth using only when the problem it removes is bigger than the indirection it adds.
User interface design starts with analysis of users, tasks, content and environment, then applies the three golden rules: user in control, low memory load, consistency.
Each UML diagram answers exactly one question; drawing all of them for a small system wastes time, drawing none loses the design.
bank_note: Long answers here usually ask you to define the design concepts, draw and explain a named architecture or pattern, and then justify the choice against quality attributes or a small case study.

bank.q: Define software design. Explain the five elements of the design model and state what each one contains.
outline: Design bridges the requirements model and the construction phase
Data design: data structures and database schema
Architectural design: major parts, their roles and communication
Interface design: external and internal interfaces, plus the user interface
Component design: each module's operations and internal logic
Deployment design: which hardware node runs which component
Note that the five sub-models are views of one design, not separate documents

bank.q: Explain cohesion and coupling. List the types of each and state which type is desirable and why.
outline: Definitions of cohesion and coupling
Cohesion types from worst to best: coincidental, logical, temporal, procedural, communicational, sequential, functional
Coupling types from worst to best: content, common, control, stamp, data, routine call, non-cohesive
Goal: highest practical cohesion, lowest practical coupling
Trade-off: pushing coupling down can split one job across modules and hurt cohesion
Small example showing a change rippling when coupling is high

bank.q: Describe the layered, client-server and pipe-and-filter architectural styles with a sketch, one example each, and one advantage and one drawback each.
outline: Layered: layers offer services downwards only; example: presentation-logic-data; advantage: replaceable layers; drawback: a request crosses many layers
Client-server: shared server, many clients, protocol as contract; example: a ticket-booking server; advantage: central data; drawback: server is a single point of failure
Pipe-filter: independent filters, pipes carry the stream; example: compiler passes or a log analyser; advantage: filters reused and reordered; drawback: poor fit for interactive dialogue
Correct symbols: boxes for components, arrows for allowed calls or data flow

bank.q: State the three golden rules of user interface design and give two concrete rules or interface features that follow from each.
outline: Rule 1, user in control: undo and cancel, no forced path, sensible defaults, user chooses modes
Rule 2, reduce memory load: recognition over recall, defaults, short menus, progressive disclosure, keep context visible
Rule 3, consistency: same words, same colours, same placement across screens; follow platform conventions
Interface features such as menus, scroll bars, windows, buttons, icons, panels and error messages placed under the right rule
Error messages should say what went wrong and what to do next, in plain words

bank.q: Draw a UML class diagram for a library lending system with at least five classes. Show attributes, operations, one generalisation, one aggregation and multiplicities.
outline: Classes such as Member, Book, Copy, Loan, Librarian with attributes and operations
Correct notation: class box with three compartments
Generalisation arrow with a hollow triangle pointing to the parent
Aggregation with hollow diamond, composition with filled diamond, direction stated
Multiplicity written at both ends, e.g. one Member can hold 0..* Loans
Association names and role names where they clarify meaning

bank.q: Draw a sequence diagram for withdrawing cash from an ATM and explain the equivalent collaboration (communication) diagram for the same scenario.
outline: Lifelines for Customer, CardReader/UI, ATMController, Account, CashDispenser
Time runs downwards; messages are horizontal arrows in order
Return messages shown with dashed arrows
Activation bars show when an object is busy
Collaboration diagram keeps the same objects but numbers the messages instead of showing time down the page
Note the equivalence: one can be derived from the other

bank.q: A college wants a web portal where students register for courses. Apply the MVC pattern and show which class belongs to which part, then draw the class diagram of the model.
outline: Model: Student, Course, Registration plus rules such as seat limit and prerequisite check
View: registration page, timetable page; no business rules inside the view
Controller: handles the submit request, validates input, calls the model, selects the next view
Why the split helps: a new mobile view needs no change to the model
Class diagram of the model with multiplicities, e.g. Student 1 — 0..* Registration

bank.q: Draw an activity diagram with swimlanes for an online order: customer places order, payment is verified, warehouse packs, courier delivers. Mark the initial node, a decision with guards, a fork and a final node.
outline: Initial node as a filled circle, final node as a bull's-eye
Actions in rounded rectangles, one swimlane per actor: Customer, Payment, Warehouse, Courier
Decision diamond with guarded outgoing edges, e.g. [payment ok] and [payment failed]
Fork and join bars for actions that happen in parallel
Arrows show the order of actions; swimlane shows who is responsible
Correct use of guard conditions in square brackets

bank.q: A railway reservation system must handle heavy peak load, stay correct on money and seats, and be maintained for years. Evaluate two architectural styles for it and recommend one with reasons tied to quality attributes.
outline: Name the quality attributes at stake: performance, reliability, security, maintainability, scalability
Evaluate layered: clean separation, easy maintenance, but extra layers cost latency
Evaluate client-server or a tiered variant: central data keeps seat and money state consistent, clients stay thin
Discuss single point of failure and the fix — replication, clustering
Weigh trade-offs explicitly rather than declaring one style best
State the recommendation with the attributes it satisfies and the ones it sacrifices

bank.q: Compare the pipe-and-filter style with the layered style for a log-analysis tool and for an interactive banking app. Say which style fits each and why.
outline: Pipe-filter suits batch transformation: read, parse, filter, summarise, write
Filters are independent, so new filters are added without touching old ones
Pipe-filter is a poor fit for interactive dialogue that needs a response to each keystroke
Layered suits the banking app: presentation, business rules, data access
Each layer is replaceable and testable on its own
Conclusion tied to the nature of the processing, not to fashion

bank.q: A payment screen asks users to retype the amount, remember a 12-digit reference number from the previous screen, and gives the error message 'Error 43'. Judge the screen against the three golden rules and propose fixes.
outline: Identify each violation against Rule 1, Rule 2 or Rule 3
Retyping and remembering digits violate Rule 2, memory load: echo the value, offer copy or selection
'Error 43' is unhelpful: say what failed and what to do, in plain language
No visible cancel or back path can violate Rule 1, user in control
Inconsistent buttons or labels across screens violate Rule 3
Fixes must be specific and tied to a rule, not general praise of good design

bank.q: A module in an existing system is called directly by eleven other modules and its internal data is read by three of them. Analyse the design problem, then propose a solution using the facade or adapter pattern and evaluate the cost of the change.
outline: Diagnose high coupling and broken information hiding; a change now ripples to many modules
Facade when the callers need a simple entry and the internals are messy; adapter when an interface must be converted
Redraw the dependency picture after the fix: callers depend only on the facade
Cost: one more layer of indirection, extra code, a possible small performance cost, and rewriting the eleven callers once
Benefit: a change inside the subsystem stays inside; easier testing with a stub facade
Verdict: worth it here because the fan-in is large and the internals are already leaking

bank.q: For a food-delivery app, decide which UML diagrams you would actually draw before coding and justify each choice; name the diagrams you would skip and why.
outline: Class diagram: the domain classes Order, Restaurant, DeliveryPartner and their relationships
Sequence diagram for the order-to-delivery flow, including payment and failure
Activity diagram with swimlanes for the order workflow and its decisions
State chart for the Order object: placed, accepted, prepared, picked, delivered, cancelled
Component and deployment diagrams only if the system has several services or nodes worth showing
Skip or keep minimal: diagrams that duplicate the same information, since each diagram costs effort
Rule: every diagram must answer a question someone will actually ask

glossary.def: Ignoring detail that does not matter at the current level so that the problem can be described in a few essential ideas.
Splitting a system into separately buildable and testable units with clear boundaries.
The degree to which the operations inside one module serve a single, well-defined purpose.
The degree of dependence between modules, measured by how much one must know about another.
Design rule that each module keeps its internal data and decisions private behind a published interface.
Design rule that each part of the software deals with one distinct kind of concern, such as display, rules or storage.
Improving the internal structure of working code without changing what it does externally.
A named, reusable template for the overall structure of a system, such as layered or client-server.
An arrangement of layers where each layer serves the one above and uses only the one below.
An arrangement where a server provides shared data or services and many clients request them over a protocol.
An arrangement where independent filters transform a data stream passed between them by pipes.
A named solution to a recurring design problem, described by intent, structure and consequences.
Model-View-Controller: a pattern separating data and rules, display, and input handling.
A pattern where a subject notifies a list of registered observers whenever its state changes.
A pattern that converts the interface of a class into another interface the client expects.
A pattern giving one simplified front object over a set of interfaces in a subsystem.
A static UML diagram showing classes, their attributes and operations, and the relationships among them.
The number of objects of one class that may be linked to one object of another, written as 1, 0..1, 1..* or *.
A UML interaction diagram with objects across the top and messages in time order down the page.
A UML interaction diagram that shows objects as a network with numbered messages instead of a time axis.
A UML diagram showing the states one object can occupy, the events that move it, and its responses.
A UML diagram of a workflow, showing actions, decisions, parallel splits and the start and end of the flow.
A partition in an activity diagram that shows which actor or department is responsible for each action.
A UML diagram showing software components and the interfaces through which they plug together.
A UML diagram showing hardware nodes and which artifacts or components run on each node.
A physical piece of deployed software, such as a jar, war, executable or configuration file, shown in deployment diagrams.
